sections.html:
Lorain County runs along Lake Erie in northeastern Ohio, with Elyria as the seat and the city of Lorain as the largest community. Population was estimated at 323,219 for 2025, up 3.3 percent from April 2020. A typical owned home is worth $223,200, and owners occupy 74.0 percent of 127,544 households. Ownership costs run $1,525 a month with a mortgage and $629 without, and gross rent is $966. The county holds 139,777 housing units and about 172,000 parcels.

Twenty public school districts have ground in the county, from Elyria and Lorain to Avon, Firelands, Keystone and Oberlin, so a tax bill depends heavily on which district a house falls in.

sections.h2: Who sends and who collects the tax bill
sections.html:
Both offices work out of the Lorain County Administration Building, 226 Middle Avenue, Elyria. The auditor occupies Room 200 and answers at 440-329-5207. The desk runs Monday through Thursday with a 4:30 close, and transfers stop at 4:00. The treasurer has Room 201 and (440) 329-5787, with weekday hours that end at 4:30.

Collection belongs to the treasurer, and the auditor points tax questions there. The treasurer also offers an escrow plan for monthly prepayment of current taxes, open to owners with no delinquency.

Lorain County was reappraised in 2024. House Bill 186 adds an Inflation Cap Credit that applies automatically when school-related taxes rise faster than inflation after a reappraisal. It shows as INFLATION CAP CREDIT in the Summary of Charges and corrects increases that came from the 2024 reappraisal. Anyone who paid before the credit posted needs to do nothing, because the overpayment carries into the next first-half bill. The law did not change appraised values.

A rise in value does not mean the same rise in tax. A levy raises a fixed dollar amount, and the millage adjusts as values move.

Real estate tax is paid in two halves, a first half in February and a second half in July. The second-half date moved later in 2026 because of the House Bill 186 credit, so read the date on your bill or call 440-329-5787. The auditor certifies the real estate rates for payment each January.

A late half costs ten percent under Ohio Revised Code 323.121, reduced by half if the money arrives within ten days. Title and mortgage companies that generate and print their own bills skip the duplicate bill fee.

A Complaint Against the Valuation of Real Property goes in after January 1 and by March 31. The rules:

  • Signature and notary seal are required, and owner, address and parcel numbers must be right.
  • Ordinary mail works, and the postmark counts as the filing date.
  • Filing costs nothing.
  • The county allows a single complaint in each three-year stretch between reappraisals and updates. A sale at arm's length, a substantial improvement, casualty damage or a 15 percent commercial occupancy shift reopens the door.
  • Complaints may also challenge farm-use determinations or property classification.

Local school boards may also petition the board. The hearing schedule and a case search are on the auditor's site.

sections.h2: Tax reductions that matter at a sale
sections.html:
Three programs come up at Lorain County closings. Ohio's homestead exemption removes the tax on $29,000 of market value for a qualifying home in tax year 2025. The enhanced version, at $58,000, serves owners with a qualifying service-connected disability and the surviving spouse of a public safety officer killed on duty. Eligible owners are 65 or older, permanently and totally disabled under 65, or holding a 100 percent service-connected rating. The tax year 2025 filing deadline is December 31, 2026.

  • Owner-occupancy reduction: 2.5 percent off for someone living in the house on January 1, requested on DTE 105C and frequently handled at transfer.
  • Current agricultural use value: a one-time $25 application fee, filed between the first Monday in January and the first Monday in March.
  • Recoupment: land taken out of farm use owes the tax savings of the preceding three years.

Buyers should ask the auditor which credits carry over, because the owner-occupancy reduction turns on the buyer's own residence.

Conveyances reach the auditor in person or by e-file. Mailed transfers are not accepted. The desk works Monday through Thursday, shutting e-file intake at 3:00 p.m. and the counter at 4:00 p.m. Handwritten, incomplete or underpaid forms come back unprocessed. Staff cannot fill in conveyance forms or advise on them under Ohio Revised Code 4705.01, so paperwork falls to a title company or lawyer.

Rental property adds a duty under Ohio Revised Code 5323.02: the owner names a contact agent to the auditor within 60 days of the conveyance filing, or risks a penalty of up to $150 on the parcel. A conveyance fee calculator on the auditor's site takes the sale amount and the number of parcels.

Selling with taxes owed

Call 440-329-5787 and ask the treasurer for the current balance on the parcel before you set a closing date. Unpaid halves carry the ten percent penalty, and the title company will normally pay what is owed out of your proceeds at closing. A cash buyer can close quickly, but the same balance still has to be cleared at the table.

Gather these before you list: your latest tax bill, the parcel number, any homestead or owner-occupancy paperwork you filed, and a Razing Affidavit receipt if a building came down. Buyers and title agents will ask for them, and having them ready speeds up the transfer at the auditor's desk.

sections.h2: Home improvements that raise an assessment
sections.html:
The auditor's appraisal page separates upkeep from additions. Repairs that are not part of a complete modernization can be made without raising the tax. Exterior items include painting, landscaping, new gutters, siding repair, storm windows, fencing and a replaced driveway. Interior items include rewiring, new plumbing, drywall repair, a replacement water heater and a furnace swapped for the same type.

These changes may add to the taxable value:

  • Fireplaces, new porches or decks, and room additions.
  • Added bathrooms, stall showers or other new plumbing fixtures.
  • Finishing an attic or basement.
  • A new or larger garage, and central air conditioning.
  • In-ground pools, and farm outbuildings, silos and grain bins.

An owner who tore down a dilapidated shed, garage or barn files a Razing Affidavit, DTE 26, so the building comes off the tax list. File it before a sale so a building that no longer stands does not show on the bill.

faqs.q: Where does a Lorain County tax payment go?
faqs.a: Send it to the county treasurer, 226 Middle Avenue, Room 201, Elyria, or call 440-329-5787. The auditor sets values and takes no tax payments.

faqs.q: When is the next Lorain County reappraisal?
faqs.a: The next countywide reappraisal is 2030. A triennial update comes first, in 2027.

faqs.q: What is the Inflation Cap Credit on Lorain County bills?
faqs.a: It is a credit applied automatically when school-related taxes rise faster than inflation after a reappraisal. It appears as INFLATION CAP CREDIT in the bill's Summary of Charges and comes from House Bill 186.

faqs.q: Can a Lorain County deed transfer go through the mail?
faqs.a: No, the auditor does not accept mailed transfers. Walk the conveyance form in Monday through Thursday before 4:00 p.m., or use an approved e-file vendor ahead of 3:00 p.m.

faqs.q: Does a Lorain County value dispute cost anything?
faqs.a: No fee applies. The notarized complaint must be filed or postmarked by March 31.
